commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

# Metabench

**Disclaimer**: The metabench project is ongoing. Running and evaluating models on metabench is not yet fully supported, please proceed with caution. 

## Dataset Description

- **Repository:** [https://github.com/adkipnis/metabench](https://github.com/adkipnis/metabench)
- **Paper:** [https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12844](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12844)
- **Point of Contact:** [adkipnis@mailbox.org](adkipnis@mailbox.org)

### Dataset Summary

`metabench` consists of a subset of six common language benchmarks (ARC, GSM8K, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA, Winogrande) which have been selected for being highly informative. The performance of models on the combined set of `metabench` testing items (n=858) has been demonstrated to predict the average performance of models on the full original benchmarks (n=28,632) within 1% error. We also provide a secondary `metabench` dataset which contains a strictly distinct set of items from the primary dataset (n=751). This dataset facilitates slightly less accurate prediction, but is nevertheless within 1% error. 

### Supported Tasks and Leaderboards

- `metabench_arc`: The dataset can be used to evaluate models on a subset of ARC items in a 25-shot regime. The standard benchmark metrics can be computed, as with the original ARC benchmark. Item Response Theory latent ability estimations can also be computed using the scripts [here](https://github.com/adkipnis/metabench).
- `metabench_gsm8k`: The dataset can be used to evaluate models on a subset of GSM8K items in a 5-shot regime. The standard benchmark metrics can be computed, as with the original GSM8K benchmark. Item Response Theory latent ability estimations can also be computed using the scripts [here](https://github.com/adkipnis/metabench).
- `metabench_hellaswag`: The dataset can be used to evaluate models on a subset of HellaSwag items in a 10-shot regime. The standard benchmark metrics can be computed, as with the original HellaSwag benchmark. Item Response Theory latent ability estimations can also be computed using the scripts [here](https://github.com/adkipnis/metabench).
- `metabench_mmlu`: The dataset can be used to evaluate models on a subset of MMLU items in a 5-shot regime. The standard benchmark metrics can be computed, as with the original MMLU benchmark. Item Response Theory latent ability estimations can also be computed using the scripts [here](https://github.com/adkipnis/metabench).
- `metabench_truthfulqa`: The dataset can be used to evaluate models on a subset of TruthfulQA items in a 0-shot regime. The standard benchmark metrics can be computed, as with the original TruthfulQA benchmark. Item Response Theory latent ability estimations can also be computed using the scripts [here](https://github.com/adkipnis/metabench).
- `metabench_winogrande`: The dataset can be used to evaluate models on a subset of Winogrande items in a 5-shot regime. The standard benchmark metrics can be computed, as with the original Winogrande benchmark. Item Response Theory latent ability estimations can also be computed using the scripts [here](https://github.com/adkipnis/metabench).


### Languages

All data are presented in Standard American English. See the relevant benchmark repositories for further details.

## Dataset Structure

### Data Instances

Each instance is presented as in the original benchmark, along with a `metabench_idx` and the data for each shot for cases where a few-shot prompt is provided, plus the original benchmark fields for each shot in the few-shot cases.

### Data Fields

See the relevant benchmark repositories for further details.

### Data Splits

All instances ought to be used as testing instances only. For training and validation sets, please utilise the training and validation splits from the original benchmark repositories.

## Dataset Creation

### Curation Rationale

This dataset has been created to offer a redundancy-free, minimal and general benchmark for the evaluation of language models. We foresee its use in prototyping and testing new models using a fraction of the resources that would be required for evaluation on the full standard benchmarks.

### Source Data

The source datasets are:
- **ARC-Challenge**: [https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/ai2_arc](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/ai2_arc).
- **GSM8K**: [https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/gsm8k](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/gsm8k).
- **HellaSwag**: [https://huggingface.co/datasets/Rowan/hellaswag](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Rowan/hellaswag).
- **MMLU**: 
  - Original version: [https://huggingface.co/datasets/cais/mmlu](https://huggingface.co/datasets/cais/mmlu)
  - Evaluation version: [https://huggingface.co/datasets/hails/mmlu_no_train](https://huggingface.co/datasets/hails/mmlu_no_train)
- **TruthfulQA**: [https://huggingface.co/datasets/truthfulqa/truthful_qa](https://huggingface.co/datasets/truthfulqa/truthful_qa)
- **Winogrande**: [https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/winogrande](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/winogrande)

#### Initial Data Collection and Normalization

The filtering process is described in [Kipnis et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12844).

See the relevant benchmark repositories for further details.

## Considerations for Using the Data

Use of this dataset will encourage more economical and efficient evaluation of language models, contributing to the acceleration of progress in the field towards more capable systems. Any other impacts are shared by the source benchmarks used to create it, so please see those for further discussion.

### Discussion of Biases

Instance selection in this benchmark has been biased by the population of models used to fit the psychometric models and any idiosyncracies therein.

# MMLU-Pro-IRT

This is a small subset of [MMLU-Pro](https://huggingface.co/datasets/TIGER-Lab/MMLU-Pro), selected with [Item Response Theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Item_response_theory) for better separation of scores across the ability range. It contains 2059 items (compared to 12000 in the full MMLU-Pro), so it's faster to run. It takes ~6 mins to evaluate gemma-2-9b on a RTX-4090 using Eleuther LM-Eval.

Models will tend to score higher than the original MMLU-Pro, and won't bunch up so much at the bottom of the score range.

### Why do this?

MMLU-Pro is great, but it can take a loooong time to run! So it's useful to have a smaller test which measures approximately the same abilities.

Ok, but why use IRT to select questions, and not just randomly subsample?

The full MMLU-Pro is quite math-heavy, and is designed for generative CoT evaluation. This means that if you want to use logprobs evalution (like with Eleuther LM-Eval) -- which is *much* faster, works with base models and doesn't require answer parsing -- the scores will be substantially lower. The IRT selection method favours questions that are discrminative across the ability range *without* needing CoT. The scores with MMLU-Pro-IRT are more spread out, making better use of the score range for current ability levels.

More info on the selection method: https://sampaech.substack.com/p/creating-magi-a-hard-subset-of-mmlu

content.text: I'll write the downloader: a stratified sample of about 220 unique models across the ability range, with per-item correctness extracted for all 62 tasks.

input.content:
"""Download per-item correctness for a stratified sample of Open LLM Leaderboard v1 models.

Source: public HF datasets `open-llm-leaderboard-old/details_<org>__<model>` (lighteval/harness
per-sample outputs). For each model and each of the 62 v1 tasks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag,
TruthfulQA-mc1, Winogrande, GSM8K, 57 MMLU subjects) we read only the correctness column and a
text column (hashed into a stable item key) using column-pruned parquet reads.

Output: datasets/v1_items/<eval_name>.pkl  -> {task: {item_key: 0/1}}
        datasets/v1_items/_models.csv      -> selected models with leaderboard metadata
"""
import hashlib
import os
import pickle
import random
import sys
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
from huggingface_hub import HfApi, HfFileSystem

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
OUT = os.path.join(ROOT, "datasets", "v1_items")
os.makedirs(OUT, exist_ok=True)
SEED = 42
N_BINS, PER_BIN = 20, 11

# task-config prefix -> (task name, correctness column, text column)
TASKS = {
    "harness|arc:challenge|25": ("arc", "acc_norm", "query"),
    "harness|hellaswag|10": ("hellaswag", "acc_norm", "query"),
    "harness|truthfulqa:mc|0": ("truthfulqa", "mc1", "question"),
    "harness|winogrande|5": ("winogrande", "acc", "sentence"),
    "harness|gsm8k|5": ("gsm8k", "acc", "question"),
}
MMLU_PREFIX = "harness|hendrycksTest-"

api, fs = HfApi(), HfFileSystem()


def select_models():
    o = pd.read_parquet(os.path.join(ROOT, "datasets", "olb_old", "contents.parquet"))
    o = o.dropna(subset=["Average ⬆️"])
    o = o[~o.fullname.str.contains("contaminat", case=False)]
    o = o.sort_values("date").drop_duplicates("fullname", keep="last")
    o["bin"] = pd.qcut(o["Average ⬆️"], N_BINS, labels=False)
    sel = o.groupby("bin", group_keys=False).apply(
        lambda g: g.sample(min(PER_BIN, len(g)), random_state=SEED))
    return sel.reset_index(drop=True)


def task_of(fname):
    """Map a details filename to (task, metric, textcol, timestamp) or None (non-standard config)."""
    base = fname.split("/")[-1]
    if not base.startswith("details_"):
        return None
    cfg, ts = base[len("details_"):].rsplit("_", 1)
    ts = ts.replace(".parquet", "")
    if cfg in TASKS:
        return (*TASKS[cfg], ts)
    if cfg.startswith(MMLU_PREFIX) and cfg.endswith("|5"):
        subj = cfg[len(MMLU_PREFIX):-2]
        return (f"mmlu_{subj}", "acc", "query", ts)
    return None


def fetch_model(fullname):
    repo = "open-llm-leaderboard-old/details_" + fullname.replace("/", "__")
    out_path = os.path.join(OUT, fullname.replace("/", "__") + ".pkl")
    if os.path.exists(out_path):
        return fullname, "cached"
    for attempt in range(5):
        try:
            files = api.list_repo_files(repo, repo_type="dataset")
            break
        except Exception as e:  # rate limit / transient
            if "404" in str(e) or "not found" in str(e).lower():
                return fullname, "missing"
            time.sleep(10 * (attempt + 1))
    else:
        return fullname, "list_failed"
    latest = {}
    for f in files:
        t = task_of(f)
        if t is None:
            continue
        task, metric, textcol, ts = t
        if task not in latest or ts > latest[task][3]:
            latest[task] = (f, metric, textcol, ts)
    res = {}
    for task, (f, metric, textcol, ts) in latest.items():
        for attempt in range(5):
            try:
                with fs.open(f"datasets/{repo}/{f}", "rb", block_size=2 ** 20) as fh:
                    tab = pq.read_table(fh, columns=[metric, textcol]).to_pandas()
                keys = [hashlib.md5(str(x).encode()).hexdigest()[:16] for x in tab[textcol]]
                vals = tab[metric].astype(float).values
                res[task] = dict(zip(keys, (vals > 0.5).astype(np.int8)))
                break
            except Exception as e:
                time.sleep(10 * (attempt + 1))
                err = e
        else:
            print(f"  fail {fullname} {task}: {err}", file=sys.stderr)
    with open(out_path, "wb") as fh:
        pickle.dump(res, fh)
    return fullname, f"ok {len(res)} tasks"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    random.seed(SEED)
    sel = select_models()
    sel.drop(columns=["Model"]).to_csv(os.path.join(OUT, "_models.csv"), index=False)
    print(f"selected {len(sel)} models; Average range {sel['Average ⬆️'].min():.1f}-{sel['Average ⬆️'].max():.1f}")
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(12) as ex:
        futs = [ex.submit(fetch_model, n) for n in sel.fullname]
        for i, fu in enumerate(as_completed(futs)):
            name, status = fu.result()
            print(f"[{i+1}/{len(sel)}] {name}: {status}", flush=True)

SEED = 42

api, fs = HfApi(), HfFileSystem()

    o = pd.read_parquet(os.path.join(ROOT, "datasets", "olb_old", "contents.parquet"))

# Planning: Benchmark Saturation Dynamics

## Motivation & Novelty Assessment

### Why This Research Matters
Leaderboards drive model development, funding and deployment decisions, yet benchmarks
"saturate": once frontier models cluster near the ceiling, score differences reflect noise
(evaluation seeds, prompt formatting, item sampling) rather than capability. Knowing *when* a
benchmark stops discriminating — and which design property (item-difficulty distribution) delays
that point — tells benchmark builders how to construct longer-lived benchmarks and tells
practitioners when to stop trusting rank differences.

### Gap in Existing Work
No pre-gathered literature review was available in this workspace (the `literature_review.md`,
`papers/`, `datasets/`, `code/` resources were absent), so this assessment relies on the author's
knowledge of the field. Prior work shows: (i) IRT can compress benchmarks (tinyBenchmarks, Polo et
al. 2024; metabench, Kipnis et al. 2024) and items differ greatly in informativeness;
(ii) evaluation scores have non-trivial seed / prompt variance (Madaan et al. 2024 "Quantifying
Variance in Evaluation Benchmarks"; Miller 2024 "Adding Error Bars to Evals"); (iii) benchmarks
saturate quickly (Kiela et al. 2021 Dynabench; Ott et al. 2022 "Mapping global dynamics of benchmark
creation and saturation"). What is missing is a *quantitative link* between the **shape/variance of
the item difficulty distribution** and the **accuracy level at which discrimination collapses**,
plus a direct comparison of **seed-induced vs capability-induced ranking variance as a function of
saturation level**.

### Our Novel Contribution
1. A psychometric (IRT) analysis of discrimination vs mean accuracy for benchmarks whose difficulty
   distributions differ in shape (uniform, normal, heavy-tailed) and in variance, separating shape
   effects from variance effects.
2. A real-data test using per-item correctness of ~220 Open LLM Leaderboard v1 models on 62 tasks
   (5 benchmarks + 57 MMLU subjects), estimating each task's difficulty variance and its "effective
   lifetime" (ability range over which it reliably ranks contemporaneous models).
3. A real-model seed experiment (local open LLMs, CPU) decomposing ranking variance into
   capability vs evaluation-seed components at different saturation levels.

### Experiment Justification
- **Exp 1 (IRT theory/simulation, calibrated to real data):** the only setting where difficulty
  distribution can be manipulated with everything else fixed; tests H1 (uniform saturates at 85% vs
  heavy-tailed at 95%) and H3 (lifetime vs difficulty variance) under controlled conditions.
  Note: this simulates *item responses from an IRT model*, not LLM behaviour; it is paired with
  real-data experiments.
- **Exp 2 (real leaderboard responses):** tests whether the predictions hold for real benchmarks:
  (a) per-task lifetime vs difficulty variance correlation (H3) across 62 real tasks;
  (b) resampled sub-benchmarks built from real items with uniform vs heavy-tailed difficulty
  distributions, scored with real model responses (H1).
- **Exp 3 (real seed variance):** H2 requires actual seed-to-seed variability of real models.
  We run open LLMs locally with several evaluation seeds (answer-option permutation + sampling)
  on easy/medium/hard tasks and compute the variance share of seeds vs models.
- **Exp 4 (historical leaderboard dynamics):** uses dated v1 leaderboard scores (7k submissions)
  to show real saturation trajectories (top-k spread over calendar time) for the 6 benchmarks.

## Research Question
Does the shape/variance of a benchmark's item difficulty distribution determine the mean accuracy at
which it stops discriminating between models, and does evaluation-seed noise dominate ranking
variance at saturation?

## Hypothesis Decomposition
- H1: For uniform difficulty distributions, discrimination (rank reliability among a cohort of
  contemporaneous models) falls below threshold once cohort mean accuracy > ~85%; heavy-tailed
  distributions keep discriminating up to ~95%.
- H2: At saturation, evaluation-seed variance accounts for more of the variance in rankings than true
  between-model capability differences (seed share > 50%).
- H3: Effective lifetime correlates with variance of item difficulty with r > 0.8.

Independent variables: difficulty distribution shape & variance, cohort ability level (≈ time).
Dependent variables: rank reliability / Kendall τ with true ability, fraction of separable pairs,
seed variance share, lifetime.

## Proposed Methodology
### Definitions
- Item difficulty b_i: IRT (Rasch/2PL-style) difficulty; on real data, estimated by joint maximum
  likelihood Rasch fit per task (logit scale) on all models.
- Cohort: K contemporaneous models with abilities within a window (sim: θ ~ N(μ_t, σ_c);
  real: sliding window over models sorted by an external ability composite).
- Discrimination D: (sim) Kendall τ between observed scores and true θ; also reliability
  ρ = Var(true score)/Var(observed score). (real) split-half reliability of cohort scores,
  Spearman–Brown corrected, using equal-size item subsamples.
- Saturation point: cohort mean accuracy at which D falls below threshold (τ<0.5 primary; ρ<0.5).
- Effective lifetime: length of the ability interval (logits; maps to time under linear progress)
  over which D ≥ threshold.

### Experimental Steps
1. Exp 1: Rasch/2PL simulation; 5 distribution families (point-mass/narrow, uniform, normal,
   Laplace, Student-t3, log-normal-skewed hard tail) × matched-variance and natural-variance
   settings; cohort of K=20 models; N=500 items; 200 replicates per cohort level; sweep μ_t.
   Lifetime vs SD(b) across 300 random benchmark configs → Pearson r.
2. Exp 2: download per-item results; build response matrices; fit Rasch per task; compute
   difficulty variance; sliding-cohort split-half reliability vs cohort mean accuracy; lifetime;
   correlation (with bootstrap CI), controlling for #items. Resampled real-item benchmarks with
   prescribed difficulty distributions.
3. Exp 3: local LLMs (Qwen2.5 0.5B/1.5B/3B, Qwen3, SmolLM2, Phi-3.5 …) on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge,
   MMLU subset; S seeds (option permutation, temperature-1 sampling); variance components via
   two-way decomposition; ranking flip rates; repeated for saturated vs non-saturated subsets.
4. Exp 4: leaderboard history: monthly top-k spread & rank stability per benchmark.

### Baselines
- Point-mass ("all items equally hard") and normal distributions as reference shapes.
- Random-item-subset benchmarks (natural difficulty distribution) as baseline for resampling.
- Bootstrap item-sampling noise as baseline noise source for seed analysis.

### Statistical Analysis Plan
Pearson & Spearman correlations with bootstrap 95% CIs (2000 resamples); partial correlation
controlling for number of items/base rate; variance components with bootstrap CIs; α = 0.05;
Holm correction where multiple tests are reported together.

## Expected Outcomes
Supporting H1: crossover accuracy uniform ≈ 85%, heavy-tailed ≈ 95%. Refuting: similar crossover,
or ordering driven only by variance not shape. H2: seed share > 0.5 when cohort mean acc ≥ 90%.
H3: r > 0.8 between lifetime and Var(b).

## Timeline
Setup+data 45 min; Exp1 30 min; Exp2 60 min; Exp3 90 min (CPU-bound, runs in background);
Exp4 20 min; analysis+report 60 min.

## Potential Challenges
- No API keys → real-LLM seed experiment must run locally on CPU (small models only).
- v2 leaderboard details gated → use v1 (public).
- Real tasks measure different abilities; cohort ordering uses an external composite (leave-task-out).
- Rasch is a simplification (no guessing parameter); 4-option MC has 25% chance floor — handled by
  3PL-style guessing in simulation sensitivity check.

## Success Criteria
All three sub-hypotheses tested with quantitative criteria on both controlled and real data, with
honest reporting of where they hold or fail.

# Planning: Benchmark Saturation Dynamics

## Motivation & Novelty Assessment

### Why This Research Matters
Leaderboards drive model development, funding and deployment decisions, yet benchmarks
"saturate": once frontier models cluster near the ceiling, score differences reflect noise
(evaluation seeds, prompt formatting, item sampling) rather than capability. Knowing *when* a
benchmark stops discriminating — and which design property (item-difficulty distribution) delays
that point — tells benchmark builders how to construct longer-lived benchmarks and tells
practitioners when to stop trusting rank differences.

### Gap in Existing Work
No pre-gathered literature review was available in this workspace (the `literature_review.md`,
`papers/`, `datasets/`, `code/` resources were absent), so this assessment relies on the author's
knowledge of the field. Prior work shows: (i) IRT can compress benchmarks (tinyBenchmarks, Polo et
al. 2024; metabench, Kipnis et al. 2024) and items differ greatly in informativeness;
(ii) evaluation scores have non-trivial seed / prompt variance (Madaan et al. 2024 "Quantifying
Variance in Evaluation Benchmarks"; Miller 2024 "Adding Error Bars to Evals"); (iii) benchmarks
saturate quickly (Kiela et al. 2021 Dynabench; Ott et al. 2022 "Mapping global dynamics of benchmark
creation and saturation"). What is missing is a *quantitative link* between the **shape/variance of
the item difficulty distribution** and the **accuracy level at which discrimination collapses**,
plus a direct comparison of **seed-induced vs capability-induced ranking variance as a function of
saturation level**.

### Our Novel Contribution
1. A psychometric (IRT) analysis of discrimination vs mean accuracy for benchmarks whose difficulty
   distributions differ in shape (uniform, normal, heavy-tailed) and in variance, separating shape
   effects from variance effects.
2. A real-data test using per-item correctness of ~220 Open LLM Leaderboard v1 models on 62 tasks
   (5 benchmarks + 57 MMLU subjects), estimating each task's difficulty variance and its "effective
   lifetime" (ability range over which it reliably ranks contemporaneous models).
3. A real-model seed experiment (local open LLMs, CPU) decomposing ranking variance into
   capability vs evaluation-seed components at different saturation levels.

### Experiment Justification
- **Exp 1 (IRT theory/simulation, calibrated to real data):** the only setting where difficulty
  distribution can be manipulated with everything else fixed; tests H1 (uniform saturates at 85% vs
  heavy-tailed at 95%) and H3 (lifetime vs difficulty variance) under controlled conditions.
  Note: this simulates *item responses from an IRT model*, not LLM behaviour; it is paired with
  real-data experiments.
- **Exp 2 (real leaderboard responses):** tests whether the predictions hold for real benchmarks:
  (a) per-task lifetime vs difficulty variance correlation (H3) across 62 real tasks;
  (b) resampled sub-benchmarks built from real items with uniform vs heavy-tailed difficulty
  distributions, scored with real model responses (H1).
- **Exp 3 (real seed variance):** H2 requires actual seed-to-seed variability of real models.
  We run open LLMs locally with several evaluation seeds (answer-option permutation + sampling)
  on easy/medium/hard tasks and compute the variance share of seeds vs models.
- **Exp 4 (historical leaderboard dynamics):** uses dated v1 leaderboard scores (7k submissions)
  to show real saturation trajectories (top-k spread over calendar time) for the 6 benchmarks.

## Research Question
Does the shape/variance of a benchmark's item difficulty distribution determine the mean accuracy at
which it stops discriminating between models, and does evaluation-seed noise dominate ranking
variance at saturation?

## Hypothesis Decomposition
- H1: For uniform difficulty distributions, discrimination (rank reliability among a cohort of
  contemporaneous models) falls below threshold once cohort mean accuracy > ~85%; heavy-tailed
  distributions keep discriminating up to ~95%.
- H2: At saturation, evaluation-seed variance accounts for more of the variance in rankings than true
  between-model capability differences (seed share > 50%).
- H3: Effective lifetime correlates with variance of item difficulty with r > 0.8.

Independent variables: difficulty distribution shape & variance, cohort ability level (≈ time).
Dependent variables: rank reliability / Kendall τ with true ability, fraction of separable pairs,
seed variance share, lifetime.

## Proposed Methodology
### Definitions
- Item difficulty b_i: IRT (Rasch/2PL-style) difficulty; on real data, estimated by joint maximum
  likelihood Rasch fit per task (logit scale) on all models.
- Cohort: K contemporaneous models with abilities within a window (sim: θ ~ N(μ_t, σ_c);
  real: sliding window over models sorted by an external ability composite).
- Discrimination D: (sim) Kendall τ between observed scores and true θ; also reliability
  ρ = Var(true score)/Var(observed score). (real) split-half reliability of cohort scores,
  Spearman–Brown corrected, using equal-size item subsamples.
- Saturation point: cohort mean accuracy at which D falls below threshold (τ<0.5 primary; ρ<0.5).
- Effective lifetime: length of the ability interval (logits; maps to time under linear progress)
  over which D ≥ threshold.

3. Exp 3: local LLMs (Qwen2.5 0.5B/1.5B/3B, Qwen3, SmolLM2, Phi-3.5 …) on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge,

4. Exp 4: leaderboard history: monthly top-k spread & rank stability per benchmark.

- Random-item-subset benchmarks (natural difficulty distribution) as baseline for resampling.
- Bootstrap item-sampling noise as baseline noise source for seed analysis.

### Statistical Analysis Plan

controlling for number of items/base rate; variance components with bootstrap CIs; α = 0.05;
Holm correction where multiple tests are reported together.

or ordering driven only by variance not shape. H2: seed share > 0.5 when cohort mean acc ≥ 90%.
H3: r > 0.8 between lifetime and Var(b).

Exp4 20 min; analysis+report 60 min.

content.text: Now the seed-variance experiment script.

input.content:
"""Exp 3: evaluation-seed variance of real open LLMs (local CPU inference).

For each model, item (ARC-Easy / ARC-Challenge / MMLU samples) and evaluation seed s, we:
  * permute the 4 answer options with an RNG seeded by (seed, item) -- option-order seed,
  * present a 0-shot multiple-choice prompt through the model's chat template,
  * read the next-token probability of each answer letter (A-D) after the assistant prefix.
The stored letter probabilities allow two kinds of seed-dependent scores:
  greedy-under-permutation (prompt/option-order seed) and temperature-1 sampling (sampling seed).

Output: results/seed_eval/<model_tag>.parquet with columns
  model, bench, qid, seed, perm (json), p_correct, probs (4 floats, in presented order), correct_pos
"""
import argparse
import json
import os
import time

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
LETTERS = ["A", "B", "C", "D"]
SYSTEM = "You are a helpful assistant that answers multiple-choice questions."


def build_prompt(tok, question, options):
    body = question.strip() + "\n\n" + "\n".join(f"{L}. {o}" for L, o in zip(LETTERS, options))
    body += "\n\nAnswer with only the letter (A, B, C, or D) of the correct option."
    msgs = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": body}]
    kw = {}
    if "qwen3" in tok.name_or_path.lower():
        kw["enable_thinking"] = False  # Qwen3: disable thinking block
    try:
        txt = tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True, **kw)
    except Exception:  # templates without system role
        msgs = [{"role": "user", "content": SYSTEM + "\n\n" + body}]
        txt = tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True, **kw)
    return txt + "The answer is "  # assistant prefix; next token should be a letter


def letter_ids(tok):
    """Token ids for 'A'..'D' (first token of the letter, with and without leading space)."""
    ids = []
    for L in LETTERS:
        cands = {tok.encode(L, add_special_tokens=False)[0], tok.encode(" " + L, add_special_tokens=False)[-1]}
        ids.append(sorted(cands))
    return ids


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--model", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--seeds", type=int, default=5)
    ap.add_argument("--batch", type=int, default=8)
    ap.add_argument("--threads", type=int, default=16)
    ap.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=None, help="items per bench (debug)")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    torch.set_num_threads(args.threads)
    torch.manual_seed(0)

    tag = args.model.split("/")[-1]
    out_dir = os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "seed_eval")
    os.makedirs(out_dir, exist_ok=True)
    out_path = os.path.join(out_dir, f"{tag}.parquet")

"""Exp 1: IRT model of benchmark saturation under different item-difficulty distributions.

Item responses follow a 2PL/3PL model  P(correct | theta, b, a, c) = c + (1-c) * sigmoid(a (theta - b)).
A "cohort" of K contemporaneous models has abilities theta_k = t + sigma_c * z_k (z fixed, evenly
spaced normal quantiles) and the frontier location t increases over time. For each t we compute:

  mean accuracy  A(t)   = mean_k E[acc_k]
  reliability    rho(t) = Var_k(E[acc_k]) / (Var_k(E[acc_k]) + mean_k Var(acc_k | theta_k))
                 i.e. share of observed score variance due to true capability differences; 1 - rho is
                 the share due to response/seed noise (each re-run draws fresh Bernoulli responses).
  Kendall tau    tau(t) = E[tau(observed scores, theta)] estimated with R Monte-Carlo replicates.

Saturation accuracy A* = mean accuracy at which rho (or tau) first falls below threshold as t increases.
Effective lifetime     = length of the t-interval over which rho >= threshold.

This is a psychometric simulation of *item responses*; it is complemented by real-LLM data (Exp 2-4).
"""
import json
import os

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
RES = os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "exp1")
os.makedirs(RES, exist_ok=True)
SEED = 42


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- difficulty distributions
def draw_difficulties(family, n, sd, rng):
    """Draw n item difficulties with standard deviation `sd` (location 0) from a shape family."""
    if family == "point":          # all items (almost) equally hard
        z = rng.normal(0, 0.02, n) / 1.0
        return z  # sd fixed ~0 regardless of `sd`
    if family == "uniform":
        z = rng.uniform(-np.sqrt(3), np.sqrt(3), n)
    elif family == "normal":
        z = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
    elif family == "laplace":
        z = rng.laplace(0, 1 / np.sqrt(2), n)
    elif family == "t3":           # heavy, symmetric tails (variance-standardised)
        z = rng.standard_t(3, n) / np.sqrt(3)
    elif family == "lognormal_hard":  # right-skewed: long tail of very hard items
        x = rng.lognormal(0, 1, n)
        z = (x - np.exp(0.5)) / np.sqrt((np.e - 1) * np.e)
    elif family == "lognormal_easy":  # left-skewed: long tail of very easy items
        x = rng.lognormal(0, 1, n)
        z = -(x - np.exp(0.5)) / np.sqrt((np.e - 1) * np.e)
    else:
        raise ValueError(family)
    return z * sd


FAMILIES = ["point", "uniform", "normal", "laplace", "t3", "lognormal_hard", "lognormal_easy"]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- core computation
def curves(b, a, c, thetas_rel, t_grid, n_mc=0, rng=None):
    """Return DataFrame with A, rho, (tau) for each frontier location t.

    b, a: item params (N,), c: guessing floor, thetas_rel: (K,) cohort offsets.
    Uses exact Poisson-binomial mean/variance; tau via MC with normal approximation of scores.
    """
    out = []
    for t in t_grid:
        th = t + thetas_rel                                  # (K,)
        P = c + (1 - c) / (1 + np.exp(-a[None] * (th[:, None] - b[None])))  # (K, N)
        N = P.shape[1]
        mu = P.mean(1)                                       # expected accuracy per model
        v = (P * (1 - P)).sum(1) / N ** 2                    # response-noise variance of accuracy
        sig = mu.var(ddof=1)
        noise = v.mean()
        rho = sig / (sig + noise) if sig + noise > 0 else 0.0
        row = dict(t=t, acc=mu.mean(), rho=rho, signal_var=sig, noise_var=noise)
        if n_mc:
            obs = mu[None] + np.sqrt(v)[None] * rng.standard_normal((n_mc, len(mu)))
            taus = [stats.kendalltau(o, th).statistic for o in obs]
            row["tau"] = float(np.nanmean(taus))
            # probability that the truly-best model is ranked first
            row["p_top1"] = float(np.mean(obs.argmax(1) == np.argmax(th)))
        out.append(row)
    return pd.DataFrame(out)


def crossing_acc(df, col, thr):
    """Mean accuracy at which `col` first drops below thr after its peak (ceiling side)."""
    i_peak = int(df[col].values.argmax())
    post = df.iloc[i_peak:]
    below = post[post[col] < thr]
    if len(below) == 0:
        return np.nan
    j = below.index[0]
    # linear interpolation in accuracy between j-1 and j
    k = df.index.get_loc(j)
    r0, r1 = df.iloc[k - 1], df.iloc[k]
    w = (r0[col] - thr) / (r0[col] - r1[col])
    return float(r0.acc + w * (r1.acc - r0.acc))


def lifetime(df, col, thr):
    """Length of the t-interval where col >= thr (grid-resolution)."""
    dt = df.t.diff().median()
    return float((df[col] >= thr).sum() * dt)


def cohort(K, sigma_c):
    return sigma_c * stats.norm.ppf((np.arange(K) + 0.5) / K)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- experiments
def main():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    t_grid = np.linspace(-8, 14, 221)

    base = dict(N=500, K=20, sigma_c=0.3, sd=1.5, a_sd=0.3, c=0.0)
    # ---- 1a. shape comparison at matched SD, with sensitivity settings
    settings = [("base", {})] + [
        ("N=100", {"N": 100}), ("N=2000", {"N": 2000}),
        ("sigma_c=0.15", {"sigma_c": 0.15}), ("sigma_c=0.6", {"sigma_c": 0.6}),
        ("sd=0.75", {"sd": 0.75}), ("sd=3.0", {"sd": 3.0}),
        ("guess c=0.25", {"c": 0.25}), ("K=10", {"K": 10}), ("a_sd=0", {"a_sd": 0.0}),
    ]
    rows, curve_rows = [], []
    for sname, upd in settings:
        cfg = {**base, **upd}
        th_rel = cohort(cfg["K"], cfg["sigma_c"])
        for fam in FAMILIES:
            for rep in range(20):  # different random item draws
                b = draw_difficulties(fam, cfg["N"], cfg["sd"], rng)
                a = np.exp(rng.normal(0, cfg["a_sd"], cfg["N"])) if cfg["a_sd"] > 0 else np.ones(cfg["N"])
                n_mc = 200 if (sname == "base" and rep < 3) else 0
                df = curves(b, a, cfg["c"], th_rel, t_grid, n_mc=n_mc, rng=rng)
                r = dict(setting=sname, family=fam, rep=rep, var_b=float(b.var()), sd_b=float(b.std()),
                         acc_star_rho50=crossing_acc(df, "rho", 0.5),
                         acc_star_rho70=crossing_acc(df, "rho", 0.7),
                         life_rho50=lifetime(df, "rho", 0.5), life_rho70=lifetime(df, "rho", 0.7),
                         peak_rho=float(df.rho.max()))
                if n_mc:
                    r["acc_star_tau50"] = crossing_acc(df, "tau", 0.5)
                    r["life_tau50"] = lifetime(df, "tau", 0.5)
                rows.append(r)
                if sname == "base" and rep < 3:
                    df["family"], df["rep"] = fam, rep
                    curve_rows.append(df)
        print("done setting", sname, flush=True)
    shape = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    shape.to_csv(os.path.join(RES, "shape_comparison.csv"), index=False)
    pd.concat(curve_rows).to_csv(os.path.join(RES, "base_curves.csv"), index=False)

    # ---- 1b. lifetime vs difficulty variance across random benchmark configurations
    rows = []
    th_rel = cohort(base["K"], base["sigma_c"])
    for i in range(600):
        fam = rng.choice(FAMILIES[1:])
        sd = float(np.exp(rng.uniform(np.log(0.25), np.log(4.0))))
        N = int(rng.choice([100, 250, 500, 1000]))
        b = draw_difficulties(fam, N, sd, rng)
        a = np.exp(rng.normal(0, base["a_sd"], N))
        df = curves(b, a, 0.0, th_rel, t_grid)
        q = np.quantile(b, [0.05, 0.25, 0.75, 0.95])
        rows.append(dict(family=fam, sd_target=sd, N=N, var_b=float(b.var()), sd_b=float(b.std()),
                         iqr_b=float(q[2] - q[1]), range90_b=float(q[3] - q[0]),
                         kurt_b=float(stats.kurtosis(b)), skew_b=float(stats.skew(b)),
                         life_rho50=lifetime(df, "rho", 0.5), life_rho70=lifetime(df, "rho", 0.7),
                         acc_star_rho50=crossing_acc(df, "rho", 0.5)))
    life = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    life.to_csv(os.path.join(RES, "lifetime_configs.csv"), index=False)

    # ---- summaries
    summ = (shape.groupby(["setting", "family"])
            [["acc_star_rho50", "acc_star_rho70", "acc_star_tau50", "life_rho50", "sd_b"]]
            .agg(["mean", "std"]).round(4))
    summ.to_csv(os.path.join(RES, "shape_summary.csv"))
    corr = {}
    for x in ["var_b", "sd_b", "iqr_b", "range90_b"]:
        for y in ["life_rho50", "life_rho70"]:
            r, p = stats.pearsonr(life[x], life[y])
            rs, _ = stats.spearmanr(life[x], life[y])
            corr[f"{x}~{y}"] = dict(pearson=r, p=p, spearman=rs)
    # within N=500 only (removes N as a nuisance factor)
    sub = life[life.N == 500]
    for x in ["var_b", "sd_b", "range90_b"]:
        r, p = stats.pearsonr(sub[x], sub["life_rho50"])
        corr[f"N500:{x}~life_rho50"] = dict(pearson=r, p=p, spearman=stats.spearmanr(sub[x], sub["life_rho50"]).statistic)
    json.dump(corr, open(os.path.join(RES, "lifetime_correlations.json"), "w"), indent=2)
    print(summ.xs("base", level="setting"))
    print(json.dumps(corr, indent=1))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

                 i.e. share of observed score variance due to true capability differences; 1 - rho is
                 the share due to response/seed noise (each re-run draws fresh Bernoulli responses).
  Kendall tau    tau(t) = E[tau(observed scores, theta)] estimated with R Monte-Carlo replicates.

Saturation accuracy A* = mean accuracy at which rho (or tau) first falls below threshold as t increases.
Effective lifetime     = length of the t-interval over which rho >= threshold.

This is a psychometric simulation of *item responses*; it is complemented by real-LLM data (Exp 2-4).
"""
import json
import os

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
RES = os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "exp1")
os.makedirs(RES, exist_ok=True)
SEED = 42


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- difficulty distributions
def draw_difficulties(family, n, sd, rng):
    """Draw n item difficulties with standard deviation `sd` (location 0) from a shape family."""
    if family == "point":          # all items (almost) equally hard
        z = rng.normal(0, 0.02, n) / 1.0
        return z  # sd fixed ~0 regardless of `sd`
    if family == "uniform":
        z = rng.uniform(-np.sqrt(3), np.sqrt(3), n)
    elif family == "normal":
        z = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
    elif family == "laplace":
        z = rng.laplace(0, 1 / np.sqrt(2), n)
    elif family == "t3":           # heavy, symmetric tails (variance-standardised)
        z = rng.standard_t(3, n) / np.sqrt(3)
    elif family == "lognormal_hard":  # right-skewed: long tail of very hard items
        x = rng.lognormal(0, 1, n)
        z = (x - np.exp(0.5)) / np.sqrt((np.e - 1) * np.e)
    elif family == "lognormal_easy":  # left-skewed: long tail of very easy items
        x = rng.lognormal(0, 1, n)
        z = -(x - np.exp(0.5)) / np.sqrt((np.e - 1) * np.e)
    else:
        raise ValueError(family)
    return z * sd


FAMILIES = ["point", "uniform", "normal", "laplace", "t3", "lognormal_hard", "lognormal_easy"]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- core computation
def curves(b, a, c, thetas_rel, t_grid, n_mc=0, rng=None):
    """Return DataFrame with A, rho, (tau) for each frontier location t.

    b, a: item params (N,), c: guessing floor, thetas_rel: (K,) cohort offsets.
    Uses exact Poisson-binomial mean/variance; tau via MC with normal approximation of scores.
    """
    out = []
    for t in t_grid:
        th = t + thetas_rel                                  # (K,)
        P = c + (1 - c) / (1 + np.exp(-a[None] * (th[:, None] - b[None])))  # (K, N)
        N = P.shape[1]
        mu = P.mean(1)                                       # expected accuracy per model
        v = (P * (1 - P)).sum(1) / N ** 2                    # response-noise variance of accuracy
        sig = mu.var(ddof=1)
        noise = v.mean()
        rho = sig / (sig + noise) if sig + noise > 0 else 0.0
        row = dict(t=t, acc=mu.mean(), rho=rho, signal_var=sig, noise_var=noise)
        if n_mc:
            obs = mu[None] + np.sqrt(v)[None] * rng.standard_normal((n_mc, len(mu)))

            row["p_top1"] = float(np.mean(obs.argmax(1) == np.argmax(th)))
        out.append(row)
    return pd.DataFrame(out)

    """Mean accuracy at which `col` first drops below thr after its peak (ceiling side)."""
    i_peak = int(df[col].values.argmax())
    post = df.iloc[i_peak:]
    below = post[post[col] < thr]
    if len(below) == 0:
        return np.nan
    j = below.index[0]
    # linear interpolation in accuracy between j-1 and j
    k = df.index.get_loc(j)
    r0, r1 = df.iloc[k - 1], df.iloc[k]
    w = (r0[col] - thr) / (r0[col] - r1[col])
    return float(r0.acc + w * (r1.acc - r0.acc))

    """Length of the t-interval where col >= thr (grid-resolution)."""
    dt = df.t.diff().median()
    return float((df[col] >= thr).sum() * dt)

    return sigma_c * stats.norm.ppf((np.arange(K) + 0.5) / K)

        ("N=100", {"N": 100}), ("N=2000", {"N": 2000}),
        ("sigma_c=0.15", {"sigma_c": 0.15}), ("sigma_c=0.6", {"sigma_c": 0.6}),
        ("sd=0.75", {"sd": 0.75}), ("sd=3.0", {"sd": 3.0}),
        ("guess c=0.25", {"c": 0.25}), ("K=10", {"K": 10}), ("a_sd=0", {"a_sd": 0.0}),
    ]
    rows, curve_rows = [], []
    for sname, upd in settings:
        cfg = {**base, **upd}
        th_rel = cohort(cfg["K"], cfg["sigma_c"])
        for fam in FAMILIES:
            for rep in range(20):  # different random item draws
                b = draw_difficulties(fam, cfg["N"], cfg["sd"], rng)
                a = np.exp(rng.normal(0, cfg["a_sd"], cfg["N"])) if cfg["a_sd"] > 0 else np.ones(cfg["N"])
                n_mc = 200 if (sname == "base" and rep < 3) else 0
                df = curves(b, a, cfg["c"], th_rel, t_grid, n_mc=n_mc, rng=rng)
                r = dict(setting=sname, family=fam, rep=rep, var_b=float(b.var()), sd_b=float(b.std()),
                         acc_star_rho50=crossing_acc(df, "rho", 0.5),
                         acc_star_rho70=crossing_acc(df, "rho", 0.7),
                         life_rho50=lifetime(df, "rho", 0.5), life_rho70=lifetime(df, "rho", 0.7),
                         peak_rho=float(df.rho.max()))
                if n_mc:
                    r["acc_star_tau50"] = crossing_acc(df, "tau", 0.5)
                    r["life_tau50"] = lifetime(df, "tau", 0.5)
                rows.append(r)

                    df["family"], df["rep"] = fam, rep
                    curve_rows.append(df)
        print("done setting", sname, flush=True)

    shape.to_csv(os.path.join(RES, "shape_comparison.csv"), index=False)
    pd.concat(curve_rows).to_csv(os.path.join(RES, "base_curves.csv"), index=False)

    # ---- 1b. lifetime vs difficulty variance across random benchmark configurations
    rows = []
    th_rel = cohort(base["K"], base["sigma_c"])
    for i in range(600):
        fam = rng.choice(FAMILIES[1:])
        sd = float(np.exp(rng.uniform(np.log(0.25), np.log(4.0))))
        N = int(rng.choice([100, 250, 500, 1000]))
        b = draw_difficulties(fam, N, sd, rng)
        a = np.exp(rng.normal(0, base["a_sd"], N))
        df = curves(b, a, 0.0, th_rel, t_grid)
        q = np.quantile(b, [0.05, 0.25, 0.75, 0.95])
        rows.append(dict(family=fam, sd_target=sd, N=N, var_b=float(b.var()), sd_b=float(b.std()),
                         iqr_b=float(q[2] - q[1]), range90_b=float(q[3] - q[0]),
                         kurt_b=float(stats.kurtosis(b)), skew_b=float(stats.skew(b)),
                         life_rho50=lifetime(df, "rho", 0.5), life_rho70=lifetime(df, "rho", 0.7),
                         acc_star_rho50=crossing_acc(df, "rho", 0.5)))
    life = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    life.to_csv(os.path.join(RES, "lifetime_configs.csv"), index=False)

    # ---- summaries
    summ = (shape.groupby(["setting", "family"])
            [["acc_star_rho50", "acc_star_rho70", "acc_star_tau50", "life_rho50", "sd_b"]]
            .agg(["mean", "std"]).round(4))
    summ.to_csv(os.path.join(RES, "shape_summary.csv"))
    corr = {}
    for x in ["var_b", "sd_b", "iqr_b", "range90_b"]:
        for y in ["life_rho50", "life_rho70"]:
            r, p = stats.pearsonr(life[x], life[y])
            rs, _ = stats.spearmanr(life[x], life[y])
            corr[f"{x}~{y}"] = dict(pearson=r, p=p, spearman=rs)
    # within N=500 only (removes N as a nuisance factor)
    sub = life[life.N == 500]
    for x in ["var_b", "sd_b", "range90_b"]:
        r, p = stats.pearsonr(sub[x], sub["life_rho50"])
        corr[f"N500:{x}~life_rho50"] = dict(pearson=r, p=p, spearman=stats.spearmanr(sub[x], sub["life_rho50"]).statistic)
    json.dump(corr, open(os.path.join(RES, "lifetime_correlations.json"), "w"), indent=2)
    print(summ.xs("base", level="setting"))
    print(json.dumps(corr, indent=1))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Build model x item response matrices from the downloaded v1 leaderboard per-item results.

Quality control:
  * keep models with >= 60 of the 62 tasks;
  * per task, keep items answered by >= 95% of the kept models and models covering >= 95% of those
    items (key mismatches from format changes show up as low coverage and are dropped);
  * remaining missing cells (rare) are left as NaN.
Output: results/matrices/<task>.parquet (rows = models), results/matrices/models.csv
"""
import glob
import os
import pickle

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
IN = os.path.join(ROOT, "datasets", "v1_items")
OUT = os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "matrices")
os.makedirs(OUT, exist_ok=True)


def main():
    meta = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(IN, "_models.csv"))
    data = {}
    for f in glob.glob(os.path.join(IN, "*.pkl")):
        name = os.path.basename(f)[:-4].replace("__", "/", 1)
        d = pickle.load(open(f, "rb"))
        if len(d) >= 60:
            data[name] = d
    print(f"models with >=60 tasks: {len(data)} / {len(glob.glob(os.path.join(IN, '*.pkl')))}")
    tasks = sorted({t for d in data.values() for t in d})
    log = []
    for task in tasks:
        names = [n for n in data if task in data[n]]
        counts = pd.Series([k for n in names for k in data[n][task]]).value_counts()
        items = counts[counts >= 0.95 * len(names)].index
        M = pd.DataFrame({n: pd.Series(data[n][task]).reindex(items) for n in names}).T.astype(float)
        cov = M.notna().mean(1)
        M = M[cov >= 0.95]
        M.columns = [str(c) for c in M.columns]
        M.to_parquet(os.path.join(OUT, f"{task}.parquet"))
        log.append(dict(task=task, n_models=len(M), n_items=M.shape[1], missing=float(M.isna().mean().mean()),
                        mean_acc=float(np.nanmean(M.values)), dropped_models=int((cov < 0.95).sum())))
    log = pd.DataFrame(log)
    log.to_csv(os.path.join(OUT, "_task_summary.csv"), index=False)
    print(log.sort_values("mean_acc").to_string())
    meta[meta.fullname.isin(data)].to_csv(os.path.join(OUT, "models.csv"), index=False)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Minimal IRT fitting (joint MAP) with a fixed guessing floor, in PyTorch.

Model: P(correct_mi) = c + (1-c) * sigmoid(a_i * (theta_m - b_i))
  rasch=True  -> a_i = 1 (Rasch with guessing floor; theta scale free, in logits)
  rasch=False -> 2PL with theta ~ N(0,1) (standardised), log a_i ~ N(0, 0.5^2)
Priors: b_i ~ N(0, 3^2); theta ~ N(0, 2^2) for Rasch.
"""
import numpy as np
import torch


def fit_irt(X, c=0.0, rasch=True, iters=600, device="cpu", seed=0):
    """X: (M models, N items) array with 0/1 (NaN = missing). Returns dict(theta, b, a)."""
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    X = torch.tensor(np.asarray(X, dtype=np.float32), device=device)
    mask = ~torch.isnan(X)
    Y = torch.nan_to_num(X, 0.0)
    M, N = X.shape
    # init from classical statistics
    p_item = (Y.sum(0) / mask.sum(0)).clamp(0.02, 0.98)
    p_true = ((p_item - c) / (1 - c)).clamp(0.02, 0.98)
    b = torch.nn.Parameter(-torch.log(p_true / (1 - p_true)))
    p_m = (Y.sum(1) / mask.sum(1)).clamp(0.02, 0.98)
    pt_m = ((p_m - c) / (1 - c)).clamp(0.02, 0.98)
    theta = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.log(pt_m / (1 - pt_m)) - torch.log(pt_m / (1 - pt_m)).mean())
    loga = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(N, device=device))
    params = [b, theta] + ([] if rasch else [loga])
    opt = torch.optim.LBFGS(params, lr=0.5, max_iter=iters, history_size=20, line_search_fn="strong_wolfe")

    def closure():
        opt.zero_grad()
        a = torch.ones_like(loga) if rasch else loga.exp()
        z = a[None] * (theta[:, None] - b[None])

"""Exp 2: saturation dynamics on real LLM response data (Open LLM Leaderboard v1, 62 tasks).

Models are split into a *calibration* half (used only to estimate item difficulties) and an
*evaluation* half (used to measure discrimination), alternating along the external-ability ranking,
so item selection/difficulty estimation never sees the responses used to measure discrimination.

2a  Per-task item difficulty distribution (Rasch with fixed guessing floor, calibration half).
2b  Empirical discrimination along the ability axis: sliding cohorts of K=15 evaluation models
    (sorted by an external ability composite that excludes the task's own benchmark); per cohort,
    split-half reliability (Spearman-Brown) on fixed-size item subsamples (N=90).
    Empirical lifetime = fraction of cohorts whose reliability >= 0.5.
2c  Model-based lifetime: Exp-1 reliability curve evaluated with the task's *real* fitted
    difficulties (uncensored by the observed ability range).
2d  Correlation of lifetime with difficulty variance across the 62 tasks (H3).
2e  Real-item resampled benchmarks with prescribed difficulty shapes (H1) from the MMLU and
    HellaSwag item pools; discrimination vs cohort mean accuracy.
"""
import json
import os
import sys

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
from irt import fit_irt, guess_floor  # noqa: E402
from exp1_irt_saturation import curves, cohort, lifetime  # noqa: E402

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
MAT = os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "matrices")
RES = os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "exp2")
os.makedirs(RES, exist_ok=True)
SEED = 42
K, STEP, N_SUB, N_SPLITS = 15, 2, 90, 20
BENCHES = ["arc", "hellaswag", "truthfulqa", "winogrande", "gsm8k", "mmlu"]


def bench_of(task):
    return "mmlu" if task.startswith("mmlu_") else task


def load():
    tasks = sorted(f[:-8] for f in os.listdir(MAT) if f.endswith(".parquet"))
    mats = {t: pd.read_parquet(os.path.join(MAT, f"{t}.parquet")) for t in tasks}
    models = sorted(set.intersection(*[set(m.index) for m in mats.values()]))
    mats = {t: m.loc[models] for t, m in mats.items()}
    # benchmark-level accuracies (MMLU = item-weighted over subjects)
    acc = {}
    for bch in BENCHES:
        ts = [t for t in tasks if bench_of(t) == bch]
        tot = sum(mats[t].sum(1) for t in ts)
        n = sum(mats[t].notna().sum(1) for t in ts)
        acc[bch] = tot / n
    acc = pd.DataFrame(acc)
    z = (acc - acc.mean()) / acc.std()
    return tasks, mats, acc, z


def split_half_rel(S, rng, n_splits=N_SPLITS):
    """S: (models, items) 0/1 for a cohort. Mean Spearman-Brown corrected split-half reliability."""
    n = S.shape[1]
    rs = []
    for _ in range(n_splits):
        perm = rng.permutation(n)
        h1, h2 = S[:, perm[: n // 2]].mean(1), S[:, perm[n // 2:]].mean(1)
        if h1.std() == 0 or h2.std() == 0:
            rs.append(0.0)
            continue
        r = np.corrcoef(h1, h2)[0, 1]
        rs.append(2 * r / (1 + r) if r > -1 else -1)
    return float(np.mean(rs))


def binom_rel(S):
    """Reliability vs. binomial (item/response sampling) noise: 1 - mean p(1-p)/N / Var(p)."""
    p = S.mean(1)
    v_obs = p.var(ddof=1)
    noise = np.mean(p * (1 - p) / S.shape[1])
    return float(max(0.0, 1 - noise / v_obs)) if v_obs > 0 else 0.0


def windows(order):
    return [order[i:i + K] for i in range(0, len(order) - K + 1, STEP)]


def main():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    tasks, mats, acc, z = load()
    models = list(acc.index)
    print(f"{len(models)} models x {len(tasks)} tasks")

    task_rows, cohort_rows = [], []
    for task in tasks:
        bch = bench_of(task)
        ext = z.drop(columns=[bch]).mean(1)                    # external ability (leave-benchmark-out)
        order = ext.sort_values().index.tolist()
        calib, evalm = order[0::2], order[1::2]
        X = mats[task]
        c = guess_floor(task)
        fit = fit_irt(X.loc[calib].values, c=c, rasch=True)
        b = fit["b"]
        th = fit["theta"]
        q = np.quantile(b, [0.05, 0.25, 0.75, 0.95])
        p_items = X.loc[calib].mean(0).clip(0.01, 0.99).values
        logit_p = np.log(p_items / (1 - p_items))
        # ---- 2b empirical cohort discrimination (evaluation half)
        E = X.loc[evalm].values
        rels, accs, brels = [], [], []
        for w_i, w in enumerate(windows(list(range(len(evalm))))):
            r_sh, r_b, a_m = [], [], []
            for _ in range(5):  # item subsamples of fixed size
                cols = rng.choice(E.shape[1], min(N_SUB, E.shape[1]), replace=False)
                S = np.nan_to_num(E[np.ix_(w, cols)], nan=0.0)
                r_sh.append(split_half_rel(S, rng, 8))
                r_b.append(binom_rel(S))
                a_m.append(S.mean())
            rels.append(np.mean(r_sh)); brels.append(np.mean(r_b)); accs.append(np.mean(a_m))
            cohort_rows.append(dict(task=task, window=w_i, ext_center=float(ext.loc[[evalm[k] for k in w]].mean()),
                                    acc=accs[-1], rel_sh=rels[-1], rel_binom=brels[-1]))
        rels, brels = np.array(rels), np.array(brels)
        # ---- 2c model-based lifetime with real difficulties (N_SUB items, cohort spread from data)
        th_sd = th.std()
        # cohort spread: median within-window SD of calibrated theta (same K-window construction)
        cw = windows(list(range(len(calib))))
        th_sorted = th  # calib already in ext order
        sig_c = float(np.median([th_sorted[w].std(ddof=1) for w in cw]))
        t_grid = np.linspace(b.min() - 6, b.max() + 6, 300)
        lifes = []
        for _ in range(10):
            bs = rng.choice(b, min(N_SUB, len(b)), replace=False)
            df = curves(bs, np.ones_like(bs), c, cohort(K, sig_c), t_grid)
            lifes.append(lifetime(df, "rho", 0.5) / th_sd)       # in units of population theta-SD
        task_rows.append(dict(
            task=task, bench=bch, n_items=X.shape[1], guess=c, mean_acc=float(np.nanmean(X.values)),
            mean_acc_top15=float(np.nanmean(X.loc[order[-15:]].values)),
            var_b=float(b.var()), sd_b=float(b.std()), iqr_b=float(q[2] - q[1]), range90_b=float(q[3] - q[0]),
            skew_b=float(stats.skew(b)), kurt_b=float(stats.kurtosis(b)), mean_b=float(b.mean()),
            var_b_std=float(b.var() / th_sd ** 2),               # difficulty variance in population-SD units
            var_logit_p=float(logit_p.var()), theta_sd=float(th_sd), sigma_c=sig_c,
            life_emp=float((rels >= 0.5).mean()), life_emp_binom=float((brels >= 0.5).mean()),
            life_model=float(np.mean(lifes)), max_rel=float(rels.max()),
            rel_top=float(rels[-3:].mean())))
        print(f"{task:45s} acc={task_rows[-1]['mean_acc']:.2f} var_b={b.var():.2f} "
              f"life_emp={task_rows[-1]['life_emp']:.2f} life_model={np.mean(lifes):.2f}", flush=True)
    T = pd.DataFrame(task_rows)
    C = pd.DataFrame(cohort_rows)
    T.to_csv(os.path.join(RES, "task_stats.csv"), index=False)
    C.to_csv(os.path.join(RES, "cohort_curves.csv"), index=False)

    # ---- 2d correlations (H3) with bootstrap CIs
    out = {}
    for y in ["life_emp", "life_emp_binom", "life_model"]:
        for x in ["var_b", "var_b_std", "sd_b", "var_logit_p", "iqr_b", "range90_b", "kurt_b"]:
            r, p = stats.pearsonr(T[x], T[y])
            boots = []
            for _ in range(2000):
                idx = rng.integers(0, len(T), len(T))
                boots.append(np.corrcoef(T[x].values[idx], T[y].values[idx])[0, 1])
            out[f"{x}~{y}"] = dict(pearson=float(r), p=float(p), ci95=[float(np.nanpercentile(boots, 2.5)),
                                   float(np.nanpercentile(boots, 97.5))],
                                   spearman=float(stats.spearmanr(T[x], T[y]).statistic))
        # partial correlation controlling for mean accuracy (task location / censoring)
        import statsmodels.api as sm
        rx = sm.OLS(T["var_b"], sm.add_constant(T[["mean_acc"]])).fit().resid
        ry = sm.OLS(T[y], sm.add_constant(T[["mean_acc"]])).fit().resid
        out[f"partial(var_b~{y}|mean_acc)"] = float(np.corrcoef(rx, ry)[0, 1])
    json.dump(out, open(os.path.join(RES, "lifetime_correlations.json"), "w"), indent=2)
    print(json.dumps(out, indent=1))

    # ---- 2e real-item resampled benchmarks (H1)
    resample_rows = []
    for pool_name, pool_tasks in [("mmlu", [t for t in tasks if t.startswith("mmlu_")]), ("hellaswag", ["hellaswag"])]:
        X = pd.concat([mats[t].add_prefix(t + ":") for t in pool_tasks], axis=1)
        ext = z.drop(columns=[pool_name]).mean(1)
        order = ext.sort_values().index.tolist()
        calib, evalm = order[0::2], order[1::2]
        fit = fit_irt(X.loc[calib].values, c=0.25, rasch=True)
        b = fit["b"]
        kde = stats.gaussian_kde(b)
        f_pool = kde(b)
        E = X.loc[evalm].values
        np.save(os.path.join(RES, f"pool_b_{pool_name}.npy"), b)
        sd = 1.0
        for fam in ["uniform", "normal", "laplace", "t3", "lognormal_hard"]:
            for m in np.linspace(np.quantile(b, 0.05), np.quantile(b, 0.6), 12):
                for rep in range(6):
                    zz = (b - m) / sd
                    if fam == "uniform":
                        f_t = (np.abs(zz) <= np.sqrt(3)).astype(float)
                    elif fam == "normal":
                        f_t = stats.norm.pdf(zz)
                    elif fam == "laplace":
                        f_t = stats.laplace.pdf(zz, scale=1 / np.sqrt(2))
                    elif fam == "t3":
                        f_t = stats.t.pdf(zz * np.sqrt(3), 3)
                    else:  # right-skewed lognormal standardised
                        x = zz * np.sqrt((np.e - 1) * np.e) + np.exp(0.5)
                        f_t = np.where(x > 0, stats.lognorm.pdf(np.maximum(x, 1e-9), 1), 0.0)
                    w = f_t / f_pool
                    if (w > 0).sum() < 250:
                        continue
                    sel = rng.choice(len(b), 200, replace=False, p=w / w.sum())
                    bs = b[sel]
                    for w_i, win in enumerate(windows(list(range(len(evalm))))):
                        if w_i % 3 and w_i != len(windows(list(range(len(evalm))))) - 1:
                            continue  # thin the cohorts for speed (keep top cohort)
                        S = np.nan_to_num(E[np.ix_(win, sel)], nan=0.0)
                        resample_rows.append(dict(pool=pool_name, family=fam, loc=float(m), rep=rep, window=w_i,
                                                  sd_b=float(bs.std()), kurt_b=float(stats.kurtosis(bs)),
                                                  skew_b=float(stats.skew(bs)), acc=float(S.mean()),
                                                  rel_sh=split_half_rel(S, rng, 10), rel_binom=binom_rel(S),
                                                  tau_ext=float(stats.kendalltau(S.mean(1), ext.loc[[evalm[k] for k in win]].values).statistic)))
        print("resampling done for", pool_name, flush=True)
    R = pd.DataFrame(resample_rows)
    R.to_csv(os.path.join(RES, "resampled_benchmarks.csv"), index=False)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Exp 2: saturation dynamics on real LLM response data (Open LLM Leaderboard v1, 62 tasks).

Models are split into a *calibration* half (used only to estimate item difficulties) and an
*evaluation* half (used to measure discrimination), alternating along the external-ability ranking,
so item selection/difficulty estimation never sees the responses used to measure discrimination.

2a  Per-task item difficulty distribution (Rasch with fixed guessing floor, calibration half).
2b  Empirical discrimination along the ability axis: sliding cohorts of K=15 evaluation models
    (sorted by an external ability composite that excludes the task's own benchmark); per cohort,
    split-half reliability (Spearman-Brown) on fixed-size item subsamples (N=90).
    Empirical lifetime = fraction of cohorts whose reliability >= 0.5.
2c  Model-based lifetime: Exp-1 reliability curve evaluated with the task's *real* fitted
    difficulties (uncensored by the observed ability range).
2d  Correlation of lifetime with difficulty variance across the 62 tasks (H3).
2e  Real-item resampled benchmarks with prescribed difficulty shapes (H1) from the MMLU and
    HellaSwag item pools; discrimination vs cohort mean accuracy.
"""

import os
import sys

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

from irt import fit_irt, guess_floor  # noqa: E402
from exp1_irt_saturation import curves, cohort, lifetime  # noqa: E402

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
MAT = os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "matrices")
RES = os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "exp2")
os.makedirs(RES, exist_ok=True)
SEED = 42
K, STEP, N_SUB, N_SPLITS = 15, 2, 90, 20
BENCHES = ["arc", "hellaswag", "truthfulqa", "winogrande", "gsm8k", "mmlu"]


def bench_of(task):
    return "mmlu" if task.startswith("mmlu_") else task


def load():
    tasks = sorted(f[:-8] for f in os.listdir(MAT) if f.endswith(".parquet"))
    mats = {t: pd.read_parquet(os.path.join(MAT, f"{t}.parquet")) for t in tasks}
    models = sorted(set.intersection(*[set(m.index) for m in mats.values()]))
    mats = {t: m.loc[models] for t, m in mats.items()}
    # benchmark-level accuracies (MMLU = item-weighted over subjects)
    acc = {}
    for bch in BENCHES:
        ts = [t for t in tasks if bench_of(t) == bch]
        tot = sum(mats[t].sum(1) for t in ts)
        n = sum(mats[t].notna().sum(1) for t in ts)
        acc[bch] = tot / n
    acc = pd.DataFrame(acc)
    z = (acc - acc.mean()) / acc.std()
    return tasks, mats, acc, z


def split_half_rel(S, rng, n_splits=N_SPLITS):
    """S: (models, items) 0/1 for a cohort. Mean Spearman-Brown corrected split-half reliability."""
    n = S.shape[1]
    rs = []
    for _ in range(n_splits):
        perm = rng.permutation(n)
        h1, h2 = S[:, perm[: n // 2]].mean(1), S[:, perm[n // 2:]].mean(1)
        if h1.std() == 0 or h2.std() == 0:
            rs.append(0.0)
            continue
        r = np.corrcoef(h1, h2)[0, 1]
        rs.append(2 * r / (1 + r) if r > -1 else -1)
    return float(np.mean(rs))


def binom_rel(S):
    """Reliability vs. binomial (item/response sampling) noise: 1 - mean p(1-p)/N / Var(p)."""
    p = S.mean(1)
    v_obs = p.var(ddof=1)
    noise = np.mean(p * (1 - p) / S.shape[1])
    return float(max(0.0, 1 - noise / v_obs)) if v_obs > 0 else 0.0

    print(json.dumps(out, indent=1))

    # ---- 2e real-item resampled benchmarks (H1)

    for pool_name, pool_tasks in [("mmlu", [t for t in tasks if t.startswith("mmlu_")]), ("hellaswag", ["hellaswag"])]:

"""Exp 4: real saturation trajectories on the Open LLM Leaderboard v1 (Jun 2023 - Jun 2024).

For each month-end M, the "frontier cohort" is the top-K (K=20) unique models by leaderboard Average
among all submissions up to M. For each of the 6 benchmarks we compute, within that cohort:
  mean score, SD of scores, binomial (item-sampling) noise variance p(1-p)/N_items, and
  reliability rho = 1 - noise / observed variance  (share of score variance that is not
  attributable to item-sampling noise).  1 - rho = noise share of ranking variance.
Benchmark lifetime (months with rho >= 0.5) is related to the item-difficulty variance from Exp 2.
"""
import json
import os

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
RES = os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "exp4")
os.makedirs(RES, exist_ok=True)
N_ITEMS = {"ARC": 1172, "HellaSwag": 10042, "MMLU": 14042, "TruthfulQA": 817, "Winogrande": 1267, "GSM8K": 1319}
K = 20


def main():
    o = pd.read_parquet(os.path.join(ROOT, "datasets", "olb_old", "contents.parquet"))
    o = o.dropna(subset=["Average ⬆️"])
    o = o[~o.fullname.str.contains("contaminat", case=False)]
    o["date"] = pd.to_datetime(o["date"], utc=True, errors="coerce")
    o = o.dropna(subset=["date"]).sort_values("date").drop_duplicates("fullname", keep="first")
    months = pd.date_range("2023-06-30", "2024-06-30", freq="ME", tz="UTC")
    rows = []
    for M in months:
        sub = o[o.date <= M]
        if len(sub) < K:
            continue
        top = sub.nlargest(K, "Average ⬆️")
        for bch, n in N_ITEMS.items():
            p = top[bch].values / 100.0
            v_obs = p.var(ddof=1)
            noise = np.mean(p * (1 - p) / n)
            rows.append(dict(month=M.strftime("%Y-%m"), bench=bch, n_submissions=len(sub), mean=p.mean(),
                             sd=np.sqrt(v_obs), noise_sd=np.sqrt(noise),
                             rho=max(0.0, 1 - noise / v_obs) if v_obs > 0 else 0.0,
                             noise_share=min(1.0, noise / v_obs) if v_obs > 0 else 1.0,
                             top_avg=top["Average ⬆️"].mean()))
    H = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    H.to_csv(os.path.join(RES, "history.csv"), index=False)
    piv = H.pivot(index="month", columns="bench", values="mean").round(3)
    print("cohort mean score\n", piv.to_string())
    print("reliability rho\n", H.pivot(index="month", columns="bench", values="rho").round(2).to_string())
    life = H.groupby("bench").apply(lambda g: int((g.rho >= 0.5).sum())).rename("months_rho50")
    json.dump(life.to_dict(), open(os.path.join(RES, "lifetimes.json"), "w"), indent=2)
    print(life)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Exp 3 analysis: does evaluation-seed noise dominate ranking variance at saturation? (H2)

Input: results/seed_eval/*.parquet (real open LLMs, 10 option-order seeds x 1500 items).
Per (model, item, seed) we have the model's probability over the 4 presented options.

Seed-dependent accuracy definitions:
  greedy  : correct iff argmax option == gold under the seed's option permutation (prompt/order seed)
  sampled : answer sampled from the option distribution (T=1) with RNG seed s, under permutation s
For a cohort of models on an item set, X[m, s] = accuracy of model m under seed s:
  seed variance      = mean_m Var_s(X[m, :])
  capability variance= Var_m(mean_s X) - seed variance / S       (unbiased, floored at 0)
  seed share         = seed var / (seed var + capability var)     (> 0.5 => seed noise dominates)
Ranking stability: mean Kendall tau between single-seed rankings and the seed-averaged ranking.

Saturation is varied in two ways: (i) natural benchmarks (MMLU < ARC-C < ARC-E), (ii) difficulty-
stratified item subsets (difficulty estimated on a disjoint set of *weaker* models to avoid selecting
on the cohort's own noise) giving a range of cohort mean accuracies.
"""
import glob
import json
import os

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
RES = os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "exp3")
os.makedirs(RES, exist_ok=True)
SEED = 42


def load():
    df = pd.concat([pd.read_parquet(f) for f in glob.glob(os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "seed_eval", "*.parquet"))])
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    P = np.stack(df.probs.values)
    df["greedy"] = (P.argmax(1) == df.correct_pos.values).astype(float)
    # sampled answer (T=1); RNG stream fixed by global seed -> one draw per (model,item,seed)
    u = rng.random(len(df))
    cum = P.cumsum(1)
    df["sampled"] = ((u[:, None] > cum).sum(1).clip(0, 3) == df.correct_pos.values).astype(float)
    df["expected"] = df.p_correct
    return df


def decompose(X):
    """X: (models, seeds) accuracies. Returns dict with variance components & ranking stats."""
    M, S = X.shape
    seed_var = X.var(1, ddof=1).mean()
    cap_var = max(0.0, X.mean(1).var(ddof=1) - seed_var / S)
    share = seed_var / (seed_var + cap_var) if seed_var + cap_var > 0 else np.nan
    mean_rank = X.mean(1)
    taus = [stats.kendalltau(X[:, s], mean_rank).statistic for s in range(S)]
    # pairwise flip prob between two independent single-seed evaluations
    flips = []
    for s1 in range(S):
        for s2 in range(s1 + 1, S):
            d1 = np.sign(X[:, s1][:, None] - X[:, s1][None])
            d2 = np.sign(X[:, s2][:, None] - X[:, s2][None])
            iu = np.triu_indices(M, 1)
            flips.append(np.mean(d1[iu] * d2[iu] < 0))
    top1 = np.mean([np.argmax(X[:, s]) == np.argmax(mean_rank) for s in range(S)])
    return dict(seed_var=seed_var, cap_var=cap_var, seed_share=share, tau_single_vs_mean=np.nanmean(taus),
                pair_flip=np.mean(flips), top1_agree=top1, mean_acc=X.mean(), n_models=M)


def matrix(df, models, qids, col):
    sub = df[df.model.isin(models) & df.qid.isin(qids)]
    return sub.pivot_table(index="model", columns="seed", values=col, aggfunc="mean").loc[models].values


def main():
    df = load()
    models = sorted(df.model.unique())
    acc = df.groupby(["model", "bench"]).expected.mean().unstack()
    acc_g = df.groupby(["model", "bench"]).greedy.mean().unstack()
    print("models:", len(models))
    print("greedy accuracy (mean over seeds):\n", acc_g.round(3).to_string())
    acc_g.to_csv(os.path.join(RES, "model_accuracy_greedy.csv"))
    # per-model seed SD of accuracy (greedy & sampled)
    sd = (df.groupby(["model", "bench", "seed"])[["greedy", "sampled"]].mean()
          .groupby(["model", "bench"]).std().unstack())
    sd.to_csv(os.path.join(RES, "seed_sd.csv"))

    rows = []
    # (i) natural benchmarks; cohorts = all models, and frontier cohort = top-6 by greedy accuracy
    for bench in ["mmlu", "arc_challenge", "arc_easy"]:
        qids = df[df.bench == bench].qid.unique()
        ranked = acc_g[bench].sort_values().index.tolist()
        for cname, cm in [("all", ranked), ("top6", ranked[-6:]), ("top10", ranked[-10:])]:
            for col in ["greedy", "sampled"]:
                d = decompose(matrix(df, cm, qids, col))
                rows.append(dict(analysis="natural", bench=bench, cohort=cname, score=col, n_items=len(qids), **d))
    nat = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    nat.to_csv(os.path.join(RES, "natural_benchmarks.csv"), index=False)
    print(nat[["bench", "cohort", "score", "mean_acc", "seed_share", "tau_single_vs_mean", "pair_flip", "top1_agree"]].round(3).to_string())

    # (ii) difficulty-stratified subsets: difficulty from the weaker half, cohort = stronger half
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    overall = acc_g.mean(1).sort_values()
    weak, strong = overall.index[: len(overall) // 2].tolist(), overall.index[len(overall) // 2:].tolist()
    item_p = df[df.model.isin(weak)].groupby("qid").expected.mean()
    rows = []
    for bench in ["mmlu", "arc_challenge", "arc_easy", "pooled"]:
        q = item_p[df.drop_duplicates("qid").set_index("qid").loc[item_p.index].bench.eq(bench).values] if bench != "pooled" else item_p
        q = q.sort_values()
        n = 150
        # sliding windows of n items from hardest to easiest
        for start in np.linspace(0, len(q) - n, 15).astype(int):
            qids = q.index[start:start + n]
            for col in ["greedy", "sampled"]:
                X = matrix(df, strong, qids, col)
                d = decompose(X)
                # bootstrap over items for CI of seed share
                rows.append(dict(analysis="stratified", bench=bench, start=int(start), score=col, n_items=n, **d))
    strat = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    strat.to_csv(os.path.join(RES, "stratified.csv"), index=False)
    print(strat[strat.score == "greedy"][["bench", "mean_acc", "seed_share", "tau_single_vs_mean", "pair_flip"]].round(3).to_string())

    # summary tests: is seed share > 0.5 when cohort mean accuracy >= 0.9 ?
    summ = {}
    for col in ["greedy", "sampled"]:
        s = strat[(strat.score == col) & (strat.bench == "pooled")]
        hi, lo = s[s.mean_acc >= 0.9], s[s.mean_acc < 0.8]
        summ[col] = dict(
            share_hi_mean=float(hi.seed_share.mean()) if len(hi) else None, n_hi=len(hi),
            share_lo_mean=float(lo.seed_share.mean()) if len(lo) else None, n_lo=len(lo),
            spearman_acc_share=float(stats.spearmanr(s.mean_acc, s.seed_share).statistic),
            spearman_p=float(stats.spearmanr(s.mean_acc, s.seed_share).pvalue))
    json.dump(summ, open(os.path.join(RES, "summary.json"), "w"), indent=2)
    print(json.dumps(summ, indent=1))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
